A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GradMetaNet work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including v2's added Appendix G and checklist.

before.justification: v1 reports original curvature-estimation, learned-optimization, and INR-editing experiments in Section 7 and Appendix F.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds transfer, training-speed, large-scale curvature, and optimizer-cost results in Appendix G.

M1.justification: The GradMetaNet and GradMetaNet++ architectures, gradient decomposition, equivariant layers, transformer adaptation, and optimizer integration remain unchanged in Section 5 and Appendices B and D. The additional evaluations do not introduce a documented method component.

E1.justification: Appendix G.3 adds cross-task transfer between CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 without re-meta-training, extending the original task-specific evaluations. Existing dataset domains remain. G.1 also describes scalar FIM-trace prediction, although its claim that this matches the original diagonal-prediction task is inconsistent.

E2.justification: The original comparator panels remain. The added large-scale curvature comparison in G.1 restricts the baseline to an MLP operating on decomposed gradients, explaining that several original baselines are computationally infeasible. This changes comparator coverage for the scaled experiment; VeLO is cited but not evaluated.

E3.justification: Appendix G introduces substantial evaluation extensions: curvature estimation above one million parameters using normalized MAE, meta-training/testing at different widths and on different CIFAR tasks, and update-time/memory profiling of a roughly 117M-parameter transformer. Original protocols remain. G.1 reports a trace target despite describing continuity with diagonal prediction, so its scores cannot be treated as matched-setting changes.

E4.justification: G.3 adds tests of transfer to unseen model widths and tasks without re-meta-training. G.2 adds analysis of whether step reductions outweigh computational overhead, and G.4 examines large-model update feasibility. These address generalization and practical scaling beyond v1's retained design ablations and small-model throughput measurements.

E5.justification: The new checklist explicitly identifies multi-seed results as means with standard deviations, clarifying entries such as Table 2's previously unspecified uncertainty type. Existing run counts and uncertainty values remain unchanged. New Appendix G tables lack experiment-specific run counts and error bars; no increase in replication is established.

E6.justification: Original Tables 1, 2, and 6 and the iteration-speed results are retained. New results include normalized MAE of 0.413 for GradMetaNet versus 0.779 for MLP in Table 7, CIFAR10 training-time speedup of 3.13x for GradMetaNet + UNF in Table 9, transfer results in Tables 10–11, and GPT-2-scale update times of 1.29 seconds versus Adam's 0.89 seconds in Table 12.

T1.justification: The gradient and symmetry definitions, complexity derivations, universality assumptions and proofs, and average-gradient impossibility results remain substantively unchanged. Section-based theorem numbering, wording corrections, and citation edits do not change the mathematics.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same architectural contribution, universality and expressivity claims, three application areas, and headline empirical improvements. Transfer and scaling evidence expands the experimental discussion without redefining those core contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix G adds interpretations concerning transfer without re-meta-training and net training-time benefits despite slower individual updates. It also explicitly explains that resource constraints prevent large-scale meta-training and frames the GPT-2 experiment as update-cost feasibility evidence. The existing architectural and attention-scaling limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 documents the added profiling model's 12 layers, 12 attention heads, hidden size 768, two A100-40GB GPUs, and inclusion of backpropagation in update timing. Its checklist newly discloses a mixed JAX/PyTorch codebase awaiting release. Existing implementation details remain; this does not establish a new code release.

R1.justification: v2 adds the VeLO reference to contextualize meta-training costs and newly contrasts architecture/task transfer with DWS, NFN, and UNF in G.3. All original bibliography entries remain, and the main related-work positioning is otherwise stable.

P1.justification: The retained manuscript receives grammar and punctuation edits, section-based theorem numbering, updated cross-references, and a conference heading. Appendix G organizes additional experiments and some relocated discussion, followed by a NeurIPS checklist. The main narrative and section sequence are largely preserved.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the experimental displays with separate tables for scaled curvature estimation, training-time speedups, width transfer, task transfer, and large-model cost. Figures 7–8 and Table 1 are repositioned near their relevant discussions. The original iteration-speed table becomes Table 8, and the retained plots are reused rather than new results.

improvement.justification: The transfer tests and training-time comparisons provide useful evidence beyond v1's task-specific evaluations and per-iteration timings. The gain is limited by sparse documentation and uncertainty reporting for the added experiments, the trace-versus-diagonal inconsistency in G.1, and GPT-2 profiling that establishes update feasibility rather than successful large-scale learned optimization. The original method, theory, and principal results remain intact.
